name: Pre-workout / stim stacks

angle.text: Lifters take caffeine-based pre-workout blends to push training harder and more often, aiming for more muscle and a leaner physique. Caffeine has the strongest evidence for performance; the other ingredients show mixed results and no appearance trials exist.

summary: High-caffeine pre-workout blends for gym energy, with mixed evidence beyond caffeine.
note: High stimulant loads can raise blood pressure; contamination has been reported.
currentQuick:
Pre-workouts are stimulant-heavy supplements taken before training, mostly built on caffeine.
Caffeine has research support for focus and endurance, while evidence for many other ingredients is mixed.
How it works: Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors, reducing perceived fatigue and pain; other ingredients target blood flow and muscle buffering.
Risks and caveats: Reported risks include raised blood pressure, nausea, contamination and undeclared banned substances. The FDA has limited pre-market oversight of supplements.
deepLead:
Pre-workout supplements are products taken before training to boost energy, focus and endurance, usually containing caffeine along with ingredients such as beta-alanine, citrulline and creatine. They are sold as powders, capsules and drinks, often as proprietary blends, and the category is lightly regulated.
Caffeine is reported to improve focus and endurance, but effects of many other ingredients are described as mixed or weak, and commercial doses are often below those studied. Safety concerns include blood pressure effects, contaminated products and undeclared banned substances.

name: Body dysmorphic disorder (BDD)

angle.text: BDD is discussed in looksmaxxing communities as the clinical condition behind obsessive focus on appearance flaws, including a muscle dysmorphia subtype. It is a recognised psychiatric disorder with established treatments in CBT and SSRIs.

summary: A recognised psychiatric disorder of fixation on perceived flaws, treated with CBT and SSRIs.
note: High suicidal ideation reported; professional mental health support is recommended by clinicians.
currentQuick:
BDD is a clinical disorder in which a person is consumed by a perceived appearance flaw that others barely notice or cannot see.
It affects roughly 2 percent of people by community estimates and is more common in cosmetic and dermatology settings.
How it works: Researchers describe a biopsychosocial origin, with checking and avoidance rituals that maintain the preoccupation.
Risks and caveats: Reviews report high rates of suicidal ideation, and cosmetic procedures rarely relieve the distress. CBT and SSRIs are the recommended treatments.
deepLead:
Body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) is a mental disorder defined by an overwhelming preoccupation with a perceived flaw in physical appearance that is minor or not observable to others, causing distress and impairment. It was moved to the obsessive-compulsive spectrum in the DSM-5 in 2013, and it includes a muscle dysmorphia subtype.
Commonly reported behaviours include repeated mirror checking, comparing, reassurance seeking, camouflaging and excessive grooming. Reviews report that cognitive behavioural therapy and SSRI medication are the recommended treatments, and that cosmetic procedures rarely resolve the distress.
Online appearance communities use language of "flaws" and "ascension", and clinicians note overlap between appearance fixation and BDD; this entry documents the clinical picture only.

name: CBT for BDD

angle.text: CBT for BDD is the talk therapy people with appearance preoccupation are directed to, using exposure and response prevention to reduce checking and distress. It is the best-studied psychological treatment for BDD, with trials on symptom reduction rather than on looks.

summary: The best-studied talk therapy for body dysmorphic disorder, built around exposure and response prevention.
note: A clinical treatment for BDD, not a looks-improvement method; see a qualified clinician for diagnosis.
currentQuick:
CBT for BDD is a structured psychotherapy for people who are intensely preoccupied with a perceived flaw in their appearance. It is the best-studied psychological treatment for the condition.
It has been tested in adults, adolescents, and in app-based and digital formats, including a randomized trial against supportive psychotherapy.
How it works: Sessions typically combine education about BDD, challenging appearance-related beliefs, exposure to feared situations while refraining from rituals such as mirror checking or reassurance seeking, and mindfulness or attention retraining.
Risks and caveats: Psychotherapy is generally not associated with drug-type side effects, though therapy can be emotionally demanding and access to trained clinicians is limited, which is one reason app-based versions are being studied.
deepLead:
Cognitive-behavioral therapy for body dysmorphic disorder (CBT-BDD) is a form of psychotherapy designed for people with body dysmorphic disorder (BDD), a condition marked by preoccupation with a perceived flaw in appearance. Treatment typically combines psychoeducation, cognitive restructuring, exposure with response prevention (ERP), and in some programs mindfulness and perceptual retraining.
It is described in the research literature as the best-studied psychological treatment for BDD. A 2016 systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials examined its effect on validated BDD measures, and a 2019 randomized trial compared therapist-delivered CBT with supportive psychotherapy. Researchers have also tested app-based and digital versions and adolescent programs.
In looksmaxxing communities, BDD is discussed as a condition that can overlap with appearance-focused self-improvement, and therapy is sometimes raised as an alternative or complement to cosmetic procedures. Wikipedia notes that many people with BDD seek cosmetic or dermatologic treatment that typically does not relieve their distress.

name: SSRIs for BDD

angle.text: SSRIs are antidepressants prescribed for BDD to ease obsessive preoccupation with a perceived flaw, and are mentioned in looksmaxxing forums in that context. They are studied for BDD symptoms; they are a medical treatment and not an appearance tool.

summary: Antidepressants used for body dysmorphic disorder, a medical treatment rather than a looks tool.
note: Prescription drugs with a boxed warning for people under 25; used under medical supervision.
currentQuick:
SSRIs are antidepressants that are also used for obsessive-compulsive spectrum conditions, including body dysmorphic disorder. They are prescribed by clinicians as part of treatment for the disorder, often alongside therapy.
They are not appearance-enhancement products and are discussed here only in their role in BDD care.
How it works: They block reuptake of serotonin, raising its availability between nerve cells; with continued use the brain adapts in ways that are thought to relate to their effects.
Risks and caveats: Common class effects include sexual side effects and emotional blunting; stopping suddenly can cause withdrawal symptoms, and an FDA boxed warning advises monitoring people under 25 for suicidal thoughts. They are prescription-only.
deepLead:
Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are antidepressants that block the serotonin transporter, increasing serotonin availability in the synapse. They are among the medications used in treating body dysmorphic disorder (BDD), a condition involving preoccupation with a perceived flaw in appearance. Wikipedia's BDD article describes SSRIs and cognitive-behavioral therapy as effective treatments, and suggests SSRIs may ease obsessive-compulsive and delusional features.
They are prescription medications used under medical supervision. This article covers general information only, not dosing.

name: Mirror checking / mirror avoidance

angle.text: Forum users describe mirror checking and avoidance as habits that feed fixation on perceived flaws. Both are documented as behaviours in BDD, with CBT targeting them directly.

summary: Compulsive mirror checking or avoidance, behaviors described in body dysmorphic disorder.
note: Described clinically as part of BDD; sources on community use are thin.
currentQuick:
Mirror checking means repeatedly inspecting one's appearance; mirror avoidance means steering clear of mirrors. Both are described in body dysmorphic disorder.
Sources specific to how these habits appear in looksmaxxing culture are thin.
How it works: In BDD they are treated as rituals that maintain preoccupation; CBT with exposure and response prevention targets them.
Risks and caveats: They are described as time-consuming and linked to distress in BDD; clinicians evaluate them as part of diagnosis.
deepLead:
Mirror checking and mirror avoidance are two opposite behavioral patterns around reflective surfaces that are described in body dysmorphic disorder (BDD). Wikipedia lists repetitive checking of one's appearance as a characteristic behavior of BDD and notes that some people instead avoid mirrors.
In looksmaxxing communities the terms describe self-monitoring habits tied to appearance anxiety. Research on them is mainly within the BDD literature, where exposure and response prevention targets such rituals.

name: Reassurance seeking (rate me threads)

angle.text: Rate-me threads are used to get outside opinions on facial attractiveness and what to improve. Clinically, repeated reassurance seeking is listed among BDD behaviours, alongside mirror checking and comparing.

summary: Posting photos to be rated; the clinical analogue is reassurance seeking in BDD.
note: Little published research on rate-me threads themselves.
currentQuick:
Rate-me threads are forum posts where people share photos and ask for ratings or critiques of their looks.
Clinically, frequent reassurance seeking about appearance is described as a behavior in body dysmorphic disorder.
How it works: Users post photos and receive ratings or feedback from other members.
Risks and caveats: No studies specific to these threads were found; related research links appearance-focused social media use to body dissatisfaction.
deepLead:
Reassurance seeking, in the clinical sense, is frequently asking others for verbal confirmation about one's appearance. Wikipedia lists it among the repetitive behaviors of body dysmorphic disorder (BDD), alongside mirror checking, comparing and camouflaging.
'Rate me' threads are posts on appearance forums in which users share photos and ask others to rate or critique their looks. Published research specifically on rate-me threads was not located; the clinical description of reassurance seeking in BDD is the closest documented context.

name: Blackpill

angle.text: The blackpill is an incel-born framework holding that looks and genetics largely set dating and social outcomes, and looksmaxxers debate whether it motivates or discourages self-improvement. Research shows attractiveness affects outcomes, while its fatalistic conclusions are a belief.

summary: Fatalistic incel-born framework holding that looks and genetics set outcomes; debated inside looksmaxxing.
note: Researchers link incel blackpill communities to hopelessness and, for some, extremist views.
currentQuick:
The blackpill is a worldview from incel forums that says physical attractiveness and genetics largely determine dating and social outcomes, and that unattractive men cannot escape their position.
Looksmaxxing members disagree about it: some treat it as a premise for improving looks, others as a trap.
How it works: It is a belief framework, not a practice; members trade arguments, statistics and personal accounts about looks and status.
Risks and caveats: Researchers report high rates of depression, isolation and suicidality in incel communities, and some studies link blackpill identification to endorsing violence, though most surveyed incels reject violence.
deepLead:
The blackpill is a fatalistic worldview that originated on incel forums as a more nihilistic version of the manosphere's 'red pill'. It holds that dating and social outcomes are largely determined by physical attractiveness and genetics, and that men seen as unattractive cannot meaningfully change their position.
Its relationship with looksmaxxing is contested within communities: some members say blackpill ideas are the premise that motivates improving looks, while others argue they lead people to give up. Researchers have studied incel communities, finding high rates of depression, isolation and suicidality, and some studies on endorsement of violence.

name: Redpill / bluepill / purplepill frameworks

chain: Different views on what to improve
angle.text: The pill metaphors are used in online communities to label worldviews on dating and status, with the blackpill being the looks-deterministic one that looksmaxxing often engages. They are cultural frameworks rather than studied models.

summary: Matrix-derived color metaphors for worldviews on dating and status; the black pill is the looks-deterministic one.
note: Frameworks, not claims tested in trials; some variants are described by researchers as linked to extremism.
currentQuick:
The pill frameworks borrow the red/blue pill choice from The Matrix to label worldviews about gender, dating and social status. Red pill is adopted from manosphere circles, blue pill is its opposite, and black pill is a more fatalistic version from incel forums.
Purple pill is used inconsistently across communities.
How it works: They work as shorthand identities: members describe having 'woken up' to a supposed hidden truth about social hierarchies.
Risks and caveats: Researchers and advocacy groups have criticized some of these frameworks, particularly the black pill, as fatalistic or extremist.
deepLead:
The 'pill' frameworks are color-coded metaphors, borrowed from the 1999 film The Matrix, that online communities use to describe worldviews about dating, gender and social status. In the film, a red pill lets the character Neo see reality and a blue pill returns him to blissful ignorance.
The terms were adopted by the antifeminist 'manosphere'; Wikipedia reports the subreddit r/TheRedPill was started in 2012 and was quarantined by Reddit in September 2018. The 'black pill' emerged on incel forums as a more nihilistic variant, and adherents of related frameworks such as the 'purple pill' use their own definitions. Scholars and advocacy groups have analyzed these frameworks critically.

name: Lookism

chain: Different treatment in hiring and dating
angle.text: Lookism is the term for judging people by appearance, and it is core vocabulary in looksmaxxing as the reason many men work on their looks. Sociology and economics research reports real but variable attractiveness effects in hiring, dating and elsewhere.

summary: Discrimination or judgement based on appearance, both an academic concept and core looksmaxxing vocabulary; research reports real but variable effects.
note: Studies report effects on hiring and pay that vary by setting; communities built around the idea have been linked to health concerns.
currentQuick:
Lookism means prejudice against people seen as unattractive, or assuming things about someone from how they look. The term dates to the 1970s and is studied in economics, sociology and psychology.
In looksmaxxing communities it often stands for the belief that appearance largely governs how people are treated.
How it works: Researchers point to stereotypes that attractive people are more capable or kind, and to employers and others acting on those impressions; field experiments with fictitious résumés have found callback differences in several countries.
Risks and caveats: Studies link perceived appearance discrimination with poorer self-rated health, and one analysis of a looksmaxxing forum describes health harms from its appearance-focused norms. Legal protection against appearance discrimination is rare.
deepLead:
Lookism is prejudice or discrimination against people judged physically unattractive, and also the tendency to infer someone's abilities or character from their appearance. It is studied in sociology, economics and psychology and is discussed in hiring, dating, politics and healthcare. 
The word is also core vocabulary in looksmaxxing communities, where it is often used to describe the belief that appearance largely determines how people are treated, and as a name for the forum culture built around that belief. Some of the early looksmaxxing forums used the word in their names. 
Published research reports measurable appearance effects in callbacks for jobs, in wages and in perceived health-care treatment, though researchers disagree about how large these effects are in different settings and whether they amount to injustice. Peer-reviewed work has also begun to examine looksmaxxing forums themselves as a health-relevant online community.

name: Hardmaxxing

chain: Structural change to face or body
angle.text: Hardmaxxing is looksmaxxing slang for invasive methods such as surgery, fillers and off-label drugs, used for changes like jaw, nose or skin that softer methods do not reach. Established procedures produce visible results, while DIY and fringe variants are poorly studied.

summary: Looksmaxxing slang for invasive appearance changes such as surgery, injectables and off-label drugs; established procedures exist, but DIY and fringe variants carry documented risks.
note: Covers a wide range from regulated surgery to unregulated peptides and bonesmashing; experts warn of complications and body dysmorphia.
currentQuick:
Hardmaxxing is the invasive end of looksmaxxing: surgery, injectables, drugs and peptides, as opposed to skincare, grooming and fitness (softmaxxing).
The label spans well-established procedures like rhinoplasty and jaw surgery as well as unregulated or fringe practices such as bonesmashing.
How it works: Surgical methods change bone or soft-tissue shape directly; injectables and drugs act on muscle, skin, hormones or growth pathways. Forum users build personalised plans combining several of these.
Risks and caveats: Surgeons warn of complications, especially with unsupervised or overseas procedures, fractures and asymmetry from bonesmashing, and hormonal and cardiovascular effects of steroids. Commentators link looksmaxxing with body dysmorphia.
deepLead:
Hardmaxxing is looksmaxxing slang for invasive or medically intensive methods of changing appearance, as opposed to 'softmaxxing', which covers non-invasive practices such as skincare, grooming, clothing and fitness. 
The term covers cosmetic and maxillofacial surgery such as rhinoplasty and jaw surgery, injectables such as botulinum toxin, and the use of off-label drugs and peptides. Wikipedia and Grokipedia also list limb-lengthening, hair transplants and steroid use among practices people place under the label, and describe bonesmashing, striking the face, as an extreme and widely criticised fringe idea. 
A 2026 cross-sectional study of social media discourse about 'dangerous' facial aesthetic trends examined looksmaxxing and its softmaxxing and hardmaxxing practices, including DIY procedures, self-injection and bonesmashing. Surgeons and other experts quoted in coverage warn of complications from unsupervised or overseas procedures and of links with body dysmorphia.

name: Ethnic/genetic fatalism ("genetics is everything")

angle.text: Blackpill and looksmaxxing forum posters use this framing to argue that facial structure, height and ethnicity set romantic outcomes, and it is the stance many self-improvement discussions react against. Attractiveness effects are studied; how fixed they are remains debated.

summary: The blackpill belief that fixed genes and ethnicity largely decide romantic and social outcomes; documented as a belief, with attractiveness effects studied but their fixity disputed.
note: A belief system rather than a practice; associated communities report hopelessness.
currentQuick:
This is the blackpill idea that looks, height and ethnic background are set at birth and largely determine how life goes. Some looksmaxxing communities hold it; others have moved toward incremental improvement.
Research confirms appearance effects in some settings but does not support the claim that outcomes are fixed.
How it works: Believers point to attractiveness hierarchies, hypergamy and dating-app data as evidence that outcomes are determined by genes.
Risks and caveats: Commentators link fatalistic belief with hopelessness, and critics say the underlying mating research is overgeneralised. Associated incel communities are described as extremist by some institutions.
deepLead:
Ethnic or genetic fatalism, often phrased 'genetics is everything', is the belief in blackpill and looksmaxxing communities that facial structure, height and ethnic background are fixed at birth and largely decide romantic and social outcomes. 
Grokipedia calls this 'genetic determinism' and says it holds that genetics, especially looks, mostly decide outcomes, with personality and effort mattering little; it adds that some looksmaxxing communities have moved partly away from this fatalism towards incremental improvement.  Wikipedia notes that looksmaxxing attributes sexual success to perceived genetic advantages. 
Researchers describing the blackpill portray it as the more nihilistic strand of incel ideology. Evidence that attractiveness effects exist is reported in some research, but its size and fixity are disputed.

name: LDAR (lay down and rot)

chain: No grooming, fitness or social effort
angle.text: Incel and blackpill forum users use LDAR as slang for resigning from dating and self-improvement, and looksmaxxing communities often cite it as the outcome they want to avoid. The term itself is unstudied, though hopelessness in these communities is documented.

summary: Incel and blackpill slang for giving up entirely; the term itself is unstudied, though hopelessness in these communities is documented.
note: A term for resignation; associated communities report hopelessness and suicidal talk.
currentQuick:
LDAR means 'lay down and rot': giving up on dating, social life and improvement. It comes from incel and blackpill forums.
It is a mantra of hopelessness rather than a method.
How it works: It follows from the belief that looks and genetics determine outcomes, so effort is considered pointless.
Risks and caveats: Research on incel communities reports loneliness, hopelessness and talk of suicide, though samples are self-selected. Support resources for people struggling exist outside these forums.
deepLead:
LDAR, short for 'lay down and rot' (Grokipedia spells it 'lie down and rot'), is slang in incel and blackpill communities for resignation: giving up on dating, social life or self-improvement. 
Wikipedia lists LDAR among common mantras in incel culture that reflect hopelessness.  Studies of incel communities describe hopelessness, self-pity and discussion of suicide, though most research relies on self-selected samples. 
No studies of the term itself were found.

name: Cope / copium

chain: Shapes what people try for looks
angle.text: Forum users apply cope to sort looksmaxxing methods into those they consider real and those they consider wishful, and blackpill users also apply it to self-improvement itself. It is slang for argument, not a technique, so it has no studied appearance effect.

summary: Slang for dismissing a method or optimistic belief as self-deception; used both to rank looksmaxxing methods and to reject self-improvement.
note: A term, not a practice; no studies of the word itself.
currentQuick:
'Cope' is forum slang for something people tell themselves to feel better. In looksmaxxing and blackpill spaces it is used to wave off a method or a hopeful argument as pointless.
It can be aimed at others' claims or at one's own reassurance.
How it works: It works as a conversational label: calling something cope marks it as self-deceptive and shuts down discussion of whether it might work.
Risks and caveats: Researchers have not studied the term directly. Communities that use it heavily are linked in studies with fatalistic beliefs and mental-health burdens.
deepLead:
'Cope' (and its jokey form 'copium') is online slang used in blackpill, incel and looksmaxxing communities to dismiss a method, belief or argument as a self-deceptive way of coping with an unwelcome reality. 
Grokipedia says the term is applied to optimistic views and self-improvement efforts that adherents consider delusional, and that blackpill adherents use it to dismiss personality and behaviour as ineffective.  In looksmaxxing, it is also used to rank low-rated methods, such as thumbpulling, on tier lists. 
No academic studies of the word itself were found. Research on the surrounding communities is cited below.

name: Incel ideology

angle.text: Incel ideology is the worldview behind much looksmaxxing forum culture, centred on the blackpill claim that facial structure and height largely fix romantic outcomes. The community and its mental-health burdens are heavily studied; the appearance claims are disputed in research.

summary: The worldview of online 'involuntary celibate' communities, centred on the fatalistic blackpill; heavily studied, with documented mental-health burdens and a violent minority.
note: Classified as extremist by some institutions; most research relies on self-selected samples.
currentQuick:
Incel ideology is the belief system of online communities of men who say they cannot find partners. Its core is the 'blackpill': the idea that looks and genetics largely decide romantic success.
The term began in 1997 as an inclusive support project and later became attached to hostile forums. It shares vocabulary with looksmaxxing culture.
How it works: Members combine ideas such as hypergamy, a 'Chad' attractiveness hierarchy and the 80/20 rule, and use slang like 'cope' and 'LDAR' for self-improvement and resignation.
Risks and caveats: Research reports high loneliness, depression and anxiety among self-identified incels. A small minority has committed attacks, and the SPLC and GIFCT classify the ideology as hateful or extremist, though surveys find most incels reject violence.
deepLead:
Incel ideology is the set of beliefs associated with online communities of 'involuntary celibates', mostly heterosexual men who say they cannot find a romantic or sexual partner despite wanting one. Its best-known strand, the 'blackpill', holds that physical traits such as facial structure and height largely fix romantic outcomes. 
The term 'incel' originated in a late-1990s support project and later became attached to male-dominated forums with hostile, nihilistic and misogynistic discourse. Researchers describe a community with high reported rates of loneliness, depression and anxiety, in which a small minority has committed or glorified violence while most members reject it. 
The ideology overlaps with looksmaxxing culture, which shares vocabulary such as 'Chad', 'cope' and 'subhuman', but the two are not identical. Looksmaxxing forums describe self-improvement, and some members dispute that they are incels.

name: Heightpill / short-king discourse

chain: Height seen as a master variable
Interest in height gain and lifts
angle.text: Looksmaxxing and dating forums use the heightpill to argue height strongly shapes romantic outcomes, which motivates interest in lifts, posture and height-gain methods, while short-king discourse pushes back. Research finds height correlations with dating outcomes; their size and cause are debated.

summary: The belief that height is the master variable in dating, plus the 'short king' backlash; research shows height correlations but their size and cause are debated.
note: Research links height to some outcomes, but effects vary by culture and context.
currentQuick:
The heightpill is a forum belief that a man's height heavily determines his dating and social success and can't easily be changed. 'Short king' discourse pushes back, celebrating shorter men.
Research on heightism has reported links between height and earnings and partner preferences, along with cross-cultural differences and small effects on well-being.
How it works: This is a belief framework rather than a practice. It is discussed alongside height-related measures such as footwear, posture and, more rarely, surgery.
Risks and caveats: No direct risks from the discourse are documented in published sources, though researchers have noted that dissatisfaction with height can affect attention and mood. Height-increasing surgery carries its own medical risks.
deepLead:
The heightpill is a term in looksmaxxing and related online communities for the belief that a man's height is among the most decisive factors in his romantic and social outcomes, and that it is largely unchangeable. 'Short king' discourse is the counter-current: a mainstream, often humorous movement that celebrates shorter men and disputes the idea that height determines their prospects.
Prejudice based on height has been studied under the name heightism, a term coined by sociologist Saul Feldman in 1971. Published research has reported associations between height and earnings, partner preferences and some mental health measures, but the size and cause of these associations are debated, and cross-cultural work suggests preferences are partly shaped by culture.
This article documents how the idea is framed and what research on height has reported. It does not take a position on how much height matters for any individual.

name: Wristcel / ringcel / heightcel / ricecel

chain: Guides which traits people try to change
angle.text: Forum users apply these labels to themselves to name the single trait (wrist size, finger ratio, height or ancestry) they feel holds back their dating prospects. They are slang self-descriptions, not measurements, and have no studied appearance effect.

summary: Slang self-labels like heightcel or ricecel that name the one trait someone feels blocks his dating prospects.
note: Tied to blackpill fatalism, which critics associate with poor mental health outcomes.
currentQuick:
These are slang labels in which the incel suffix is attached to a trait: height, wrist size, ring-finger length or ethnic background.
They express the belief that one physical feature determines romantic outcomes. No studies test the labels themselves.
How it works: They are social identity markers in online communities rather than practices, and are linked to the blackpill belief that genetics decides dating success.
Risks and caveats: Critics link blackpill-style fatalism with poor mental health and, in some cases, violence. The labels themselves have no documented physical risk.
deepLead:
Wristcel, ringcel, heightcel and ricecel are self-applied labels from incel and looksmaxxing slang. The '-cel' suffix derives from 'incel', short for involuntary celibate, and the prefix names the physical trait or background a person blames for his romantic outcomes: wrist size, ring-finger length, height or East or Southeast Asian ancestry.
Only ricecel is described in the sources reviewed here, as one of several race-based variants alongside 'currycel' for South Asian ancestry and the umbrella term 'ethnicel'. Published coverage reviewed does not describe the wrist, ring or height variants in detail, so their exact usage is documented here only in general terms.

name: Subhuman / LTN / HTN / Chad tiers

chain: Rate faces on a tier scale
angle.text: Looksmaxxing and incel communities use these tiers, descended from the PSL scale, to rank men's attractiveness and to set goals for improvement. The labels are informal community ratings rather than validated measures.

summary: The ranking vocabulary of looksmaxxing: from subhuman through LTN and HTN to Chad, descended from the PSL scale.
note: Researchers consider parts of the PSL system pseudoscientific; critics object to dehumanising labels.
currentQuick:
Tier language ranks men by perceived looks. The bottom is 'subhuman', the middle splits into low-tier and high-tier normie, and the top is Chad, with further steps like giga Chad.
The system descends from the PSL scale, which scores facial attractiveness from 1 to 8.
How it works: It is a shared vocabulary, not a procedure. Members rate faces against the scale, often in forum photo threads.
Risks and caveats: Critics note the labels can be dehumanising and that the scale has no scientific validation; effects on self-image have not been formally studied in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Subhuman, LTN, HTN and Chad are labels in a tier system used in looksmaxxing and incel communities to rank men's physical attractiveness. LTN and HTN stand for low-tier normie and high-tier normie. The system descends from a rating scale developed on defunct forums.
Wikipedia's article on looksmaxxing describes seven categories in the PSL (Perceived Sexual Levels) scale, which rates facial attractiveness on a 1 to 8 scale and is built around assumptions about how women perceive men, with the lowest category called 'subhuman' or 'sub-3'. Another description of the scene, associated with the streamer Clavicular, uses three tiers: subhuman, normie and Chad. Researchers and critics consider parts of the PSL system pseudoscientific.

name: Manifestation / law of attraction for looks

chain: Feel the goal as already achieved
angle.text: Practitioners combine visualisation and affirmations in the belief that thoughts draw matching outcomes, applying it to a changed face, body or skin. No studies test manifestation for physical appearance change.

summary: Visualising and 'manifesting' a better face or body via the law of attraction; no studies test it for appearance.
note: No empirical evidence supports the law of attraction; believers show more risk-taking in one study.
currentQuick:
Manifestation applies the law of attraction to looks: believers visualise the desired appearance and feel it as already real, expecting reality to follow.
No published studies test this for appearance, and the underlying idea is described as lacking empirical support.
How it works: Practitioners combine visualisation, affirmations and an emotional sense of already having the result. Proponents attribute the effect to energy alignment.
Risks and caveats: No direct physical risk is documented. Critics warn it can imply blame for misfortune and undervalue effort, and one study linked belief to greater financial risk-taking.
deepLead:
Manifestation, in this context, is the application of the law of attraction, the New Thought belief that thoughts and feelings draw matching experiences into a person's life, to appearance goals such as a changed face, body or skin. Practitioners typically combine visualisation and affirmations, and stress feeling that the goal has already been achieved.
Wikipedia reports that no empirical scientific evidence supports the law of attraction, and that it is widely regarded as pseudoscience or religion framed in scientific language. Proponents counter with personal accounts of success. No studies have tested manifestation specifically for physical appearance.

name: Affirmations / self-talk

angle.text: Users repeat positive statements to counter negative face or body image and build confidence. Value-based self-affirmation has some research, while affirmations for looks have not been tested.

summary: Repeating positive self-statements to shift self-image; value-based self-affirmation has some research, but nothing tests it for looks.
note: Present-tense statements may backfire for people with low self-esteem (Wood 2009).
currentQuick:
Affirmations are positive statements people repeat to change how they see themselves, sometimes used for face or body image.
Research on value-based self-affirmation shows stress-buffering effects that are described as preliminary, while a 2009 study found repeated positive statements can backfire for people with low self-esteem.
How it works: Self-affirmation theory proposes that reflecting on valued domains protects overall self-worth, which reduces defensiveness under threat.
Risks and caveats: No physical risks are documented. Studies suggest present-tense positive statements may worsen mood for people with low self-esteem.
deepLead:
Affirmations are positive statements, repeated or written, that a person uses to shape beliefs about himself; in New Thought practice they are described as present-tense, positive, personal and specific. In appearance contexts, people use them to counter negative body or face image.
Two bodies of work are often conflated. Self-affirmation theory, proposed by Claude Steele in 1988, concerns reflecting on important personal values to protect self-worth, and has produced experimental findings on stress and defensiveness. Repeating positive statements is a separate practice, and a 2009 study by Wood and colleagues reported that present-tense statements such as 'I am...' helped people with high self-esteem but left those with low self-esteem feeling worse. No studies have tested affirmations for physical appearance outcomes.

name: Meditation / mindfulness

angle.text: Appearance and self-improvement communities discuss meditation as a way to reduce stress and improve self-image, which they link to a calmer presence. Stress effects are widely studied; effects on appearance specifically are not.

summary: Attention-training practice used for stress and self-image; broad stress research exists, but none on appearance.
note: Research quality is uneven; no studies test appearance outcomes.
currentQuick:
Meditation and mindfulness train attention and non-judgmental awareness, and are used in looksmaxxing circles to manage stress and self-image.
Reviews report benefits for stress, pain and mood in some populations, though a 2012 meta-analysis noted that methodological problems excluded most studies.
How it works: Practitioners focus attention on breath, body or thoughts without judgement; studies suggest effects on attention and pain processing distinct from placebo.
Risks and caveats: The sources reviewed document no physical risks. Critics note commercialisation and inconsistent definitions, and no studies test appearance outcomes.
deepLead:
Meditation and mindfulness are attention-training practices used for stress management and emotional regulation. In clinical psychology, mindfulness is deliberate, usually nonjudgmental awareness of bodily sensations, feelings, thoughts and surroundings. In appearance and self-improvement communities it is discussed as a way to reduce stress and improve self-image.
Research on meditation is large but methodologically uneven: a 2012 meta-analysis excluded almost three quarters of 595 identified studies for methodological problems, and a 2007 evidence review described the state of research across practices. No studies in the sources reviewed test meditation for physical appearance.
